chapter: Western Philosophy: Locke, Hume and Kant
trick: The three form an argument in sequence. Locke: all knowledge comes from experience, the mind is a blank slate. Hume pushes empiricism to its end: we never observe causation, only constant conjunction. Kant answers both: experience supplies the matter, the mind supplies the form — 'percepts without concepts are blind'.

trick: The Indian theories divide on one question: does the effect already exist in the cause? Satkaryavada says yes (Samkhya's parinamavada, real transformation; Advaita's vivartavada, apparent transformation). Asatkaryavada says no (Nyaya-Vaisheshika — the effect is a new beginning). Ask that one question and every school sorts itself.

video.query: satkaryavada asatkaryavada parinamavada vivartavada causation class 12 philosophy

data.prompt: Match each theory of causation with what it holds.

pairs.right: The effect pre-exists in the cause — oil is already in the seed
The effect is a new beginning, not present in the cause before — Nyaya-Vaisheshika
Samkhya: the cause really transforms into the effect, as milk into curd
Advaita: the transformation is only apparent, as the rope appears to be a snake
The material cause — the clay of the pot
Only constant conjunction is observed; necessity is a habit of the mind
Causality is a category the understanding brings to experience

trick: Advaita means 'not two'. Brahman alone is real, the world is maya, and the self is not different from Brahman — 'Brahma satyam jagat mithya jivo brahmaiva naparah' compresses the whole system into one line. The rope-and-snake illustration is asked for by name: the snake was never there, yet it was really seen.

video.query: shankara advaita vedanta brahman maya rope snake class 12 philosophy

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about Advaita Vedanta.

items.statement: Advaita holds that Brahman alone is ultimately real.
items.why: The world has vyavaharika or empirical reality but not paramarthika or absolute reality.

items.statement: Maya means that the world is simply non-existent.
items.why: Maya is anirvachaniya — indescribable as either real or unreal. The world is experienced, but it is not ultimately real.

items.statement: The rope-and-snake example illustrates superimposition, adhyasa.
items.why: The snake is superimposed on the rope, as the world is superimposed on Brahman; knowledge removes it.

items.statement: In Advaita the individual self is ultimately different from Brahman.
items.why: Jiva and Brahman are identical — that identity is what 'not two' means, and it is the whole difference from Ramanuja.

items.statement: Liberation in Advaita comes through knowledge (jnana).
items.why: Bondage is caused by ignorance, so only knowledge can end it — action cannot remove a mistake of understanding.

trick: Every Indian school names the goal differently but describes the same release: moksha in Vedanta, nirvana in Buddhism, kaivalya in Jainism and in Samkhya-Yoga. And the cause of bondage is ignorance, so the path is knowledge — that link between avidya and moksha is what most answers turn on.

trick: Two families of moral theory, divided by where the rightness lies. Consequentialism looks at results — utilitarianism's greatest happiness of the greatest number, Bentham then Mill. Deontology looks at the act itself — Kant's categorical imperative, duty for duty's sake. Ask what the theory examines, the outcome or the intention.

chapter: Sociology: Society, Institutions and Social Groups
trick: Cooley's primary group is small, face-to-face and intimate — the family, the play group; the secondary group is large, impersonal and organised for a purpose — a political party, a trade union. Community is a natural grouping with a sense of we-feeling; an association is deliberately formed for an interest.

trick: Education has manifest functions, which are intended and stated — transmitting knowledge and skill — and latent functions, which are real but unstated: socialisation, social control, and the sorting of people into positions. Being asked for a 'latent' function and giving a manifest one is the standard way marks are lost here.

chapter: Indian Educationists: Vivekananda, Gandhi and Aurobindo
trick: One sentence each, and they never overlap. Vivekananda: education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man. Gandhi: education through a productive craft, in the mother tongue, self-supporting — Nai Talim. Aurobindo: integral education of the physical, vital, mental, psychic and spiritual, and 'nothing can be taught' — the teacher only helps.

trick: The word itself is the definition: philo-sophia, love of wisdom. Philosophy differs from science by asking what cannot be settled by observation, and from religion by relying on reason rather than on revelation or faith. Every 'distinguish between' question in this chapter runs along one of those two lines.

video.query: meaning nature scope of philosophy relation with science religion class 12

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about the nature of philosophy.

items.statement: The word philosophy comes from Greek roots meaning 'love of wisdom'.
items.why: Philos, love, and sophia, wisdom — Pythagoras is traditionally credited with the coinage.

items.statement: Philosophy settles its questions by experiment, as science does.
items.why: Its questions are not settled by observation. It proceeds by argument, analysis and criticism.

items.statement: Philosophy relies on reason, while religion rests on faith and revelation.
items.why: A philosopher must give reasons that another may examine and reject; that is the standard distinction.

items.statement: Metaphysics, epistemology and ethics are branches of philosophy.
items.why: They ask, respectively, what exists, how we know, and what we ought to do. Logic is usually added as a fourth.

items.statement: Philosophy has no bearing on ordinary life.
items.why: Every view of duty, justice or knowledge rests on philosophical assumptions, whether or not they are examined.
